findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

additional_observations: Comparison: outside non-contrast head CT two weeks earlier; no change
ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait and distractibility; witnessed event with forced eye closure and side-to-side head movements
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Four weeks of right leg weakness and shaking events: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign and collapsing weakness and on the semiology of an observed event, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm with normal conduction and QT interval
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: Episodes of apparent unresponsiveness: NICE advises a 12-lead ECG after transient loss of consciousness (CG109) and after a suspected seizure (NG217). The event semiology already favours functional seizures, so it does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: She was admitted with daily shaking episodes during which she sometimes cannot respond. Recording a habitual event without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and assesses co-occurring epilepsy, as the AAN guideline advises. Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lesion explaining the right leg weakness
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: She fears multiple sclerosis or a tumor and the outside CT was normal; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, intact posterior column sensation and the positive signs already answer the structural question, so a single non-contrast scan is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bleeding risk of sertraline with as-needed ibuprofen; nothing on the list was started for the events
action_criteria.label: Review the current medicines for interactions
action_criteria.rationale: No antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine has been started for her events, so the review does not change the plan; sertraline with ibuprofen carries a bleeding risk worth noting.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her anxiety, mood and health-anxiety symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat CT after the normal outside scan, repeat MRI, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional right leg weakness and functional seizures) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility, and on the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information. Address her fear of multiple sclerosis or a brain tumor by showing her the positive signs and why they do not fit those diseases.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder and depression.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, syncope or embolic question is raised; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
The events are shaking with partial responsiveness and no syncope or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
A head CT at the outside emergency department two weeks ago was normal; repeating it answers no new question and adds radiation.
She is afebrile with no inflammatory or encephalopathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add iatrogenic risk and feed her fear of multiple sclerosis without a question to answer.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Light-touch and pinprick loss with a midline split at the groin and intact vibration and proprioception is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with weakness and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Daily shaking episodes with reduced responsiveness and a grandmother with epilepsy. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

differential.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis, tumor or another structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Progressive right leg weakness with sensory loss, and her own fear of multiple sclerosis or a tumor, raise a structural cause; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, normal tone, intact vibration and proprioception, and a positive Hoover sign with collapsing weakness are incompatible with a corticospinal or dorsal column lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility are validated rule-in signs; the midline-splitting sensory loss and Romberg sway are supportive only.

The habitual event (90 seconds of arrhythmic, waxing and waning shaking with forced eye closure and side-to-side head movements) was witnessed and recorded on video-EEG without ictal change: the ILAE documented level of certainty.

Her fear of multiple sclerosis or a tumor is answered by explaining the positive signs; the outside CT was normal, a single non-contrast MRI is defensible at most, and repeat imaging does not reassure.
A grandmother with epilepsy is a remote family history and does not make her recorded events epileptic.
Work conflict, her partner's job loss and a distressing minor car accident are supportive context; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree family history of epilepsy does not make her events epileptic; the habitual event recorded on video-EEG without ictal change answers the question.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic cause and start antiseizure drugs before the events are recorded

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder and depression in partial remission
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Work conflict, her partner's job loss and a distressing minor car accident before onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressors alone, without positive signs or typical event semiology

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal tests rarely reassure a patient with functional symptoms; showing her the positive signs addresses the fear, and one non-contrast MRI at most is defensible.
red_herrings.data_point: She fears multiple sclerosis or a brain tumor and has been researching her symptoms online
red_herrings.intended_effect: Order imaging, a lumbar puncture or evoked potentials to reassure her

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion reach 4/5 and then suddenly give way.
Right leg dragged on walking with an inconsistent pattern.
Leg movements normalize briefly when she is distracted by conversation, and right heel-to-shin varies between normal and impaired.

Bilateral arm and leg shaking for about 90 seconds, arrhythmic and waxing and waning, with forced eye closure, side-to-side head movements and partial responsiveness to voice; it settled with verbal reassurance and was followed by no confusion.
Light-touch and pinprick loss over the whole right leg with a sharp midline split at the groin, and exaggerated Romberg sway without falling; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric with flexor plantars; normal tone, no pronator drift; vibration and proprioception intact.
findings.sign: Reflexes, tone and posterior column sensation

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility of the right leg deficit. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (forced eye closure, arrhythmic waxing and waning shaking, side-to-side head movements, partial responsiveness, recovery without confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric mucosa; increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding with regular combined use. Consider gastroprotection or a non-NSAID analgesic.
current_medications.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, up to three times daily; dicyclomine 20 mg as needed before meals
current_medications.summary: One moderate interaction (sertraline with ibuprofen, gastrointestinal bleeding risk); no other clinically significant interactions among the current medicines.
warnings: Dicyclomine: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness); no significant interaction with sertraline at as-needed doses.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes, no abnormal response, did not provoke clinical event
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Normal photic driving response, no photoparoxysmal response

artifacts.description: Present during the event; underlying cerebral activity discernible between bursts.

background.overall: Continuous inpatient video-EEG for 24 hours, international 10-20 system. Normal, symmetric background in wakefulness and sleep.
background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz symmetric alpha rhythm, well-modulated and reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_architecture: Normal sleep transients: vertex waves in drowsiness, sleep spindles and K-complexes in stage N2 sleep

findings.morphology: Bilateral arm and leg shaking, arrhythmic and waxing and waning, with forced eye closure and side-to-side head movements, lasting 1 min 30 s; she answered to her name during parts of the event. Muscle artifact over the temporal channels; the posterior alpha rhythm remained visible. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. One habitual event was recorded (bilateral arm and leg shaking with forced eye closure, 1 min 30 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the event; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the event. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lauren Hadley is a 28-year-old right-handed woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a four-week history of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of whole-body shaking. The symptoms began approximately four weeks ago when she noticed her right leg 'giving out' while walking up stairs at work. Over the following week the weakness progressed to the point where she had difficulty walking without a limp, and she has been using a cane for the past two weeks. She reports the leg feels 'dead' and she cannot control it. She also describes decreased sensation over the entire right leg, stating it feels numb from the hip down. Concurrently, she began experiencing episodes of shaking approximately three weeks ago. These episodes involve bilateral arm and leg trembling, sometimes with her eyes rolling back. They last between one and three minutes. During some episodes she reports being able to hear people around her but is unable to respond. There is no tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-ictal confusion. The episodes occur one to two times per day and seem to be triggered by emotional stress or fatigue. She was seen at an outside emergency department two weeks ago where a CT head was normal and she was referred for outpatient neurology follow-up, but her symptoms worsened and she was admitted for further evaluation including video-EEG monitoring. She reports significant psychosocial stress including workplace conflict with a new supervisor, her partner's recent unemployment, and a minor motor vehicle accident six weeks ago that she found very distressing despite no physical injury. She denies any prior history of seizures, stroke, or neurological disease. She has been taking sertraline for anxiety and depression. She is very concerned she may have multiple sclerosis or a brain tumor and has been researching her symptoms extensively online.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper and lower extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds. Eyes were noted to be forcefully closed during the event. The shaking was arrhythmic, waxing and waning, with side-to-side head movements. She remained responsive to voice during portions of the event. No post-ictal confusion, no cyanosis, no tongue biting, no incontinence. The episode self-resolved with verbal reassurance. Video-EEG was being recorded during this event.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal on the left. On the right, patient demonstrates inconsistent performance with moments of normal coordination interspersed with apparent difficulty. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient initially states she cannot walk. When assisted to standing, demonstrates a dragging gait of the right leg with inconsistent pattern. When distracted by conversation, leg movements briefly normalize. No Trendelenburg sign. Tandem gait not attempted due to patient's reported inability. Romberg testing: dramatic swaying without falling, with ability to self-correct. Overall gait pattern is non-physiologic.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent with normal rate, rhythm, and prosody. No dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact, able to spell WORLD backwards and perform serial sevens without error. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. Affect is somewhat flat but cooperative. She appears anxious and focused on her leg symptoms.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no spasticity or rigidity. Upper extremities: strength 5/5 bilaterally in all muscle groups (deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, grip). Right lower extremity: give-way weakness in hip flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion; the patient initiates movement to 4/5 then suddenly gives way. Left lower extremity: 5/5 in all muscle groups. Hoover sign positive on the right: right hip extension is weak on direct testing but becomes full when she flexes the left hip against resistance. No pronator drift. No muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. Reflexes are symmetric and normal, inconsistent with upper or lower motor neuron lesion.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the entire right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution with a sharp midline split at the groin. Vibration and proprioception intact throughout. Sensory findings do not conform to any peripheral nerve, root, or spinal cord pattern.
